scenes.script_line: Imagine that five people walk past the same piece of litter. The first is busy. The second does not notice it. The third thinks, "It is not mine." The fourth assumes someone else will collect it. And the fifth sees it, but does not know where to put it. Five people. One small problem. And the litter is still there.

shots.text: wide shot of several workers walking past a piece of litter beside a path, one after another
close-up of a piece of light plastic caught beside a busy path
worker glancing at litter but continuing to walk, unsure what to do
medium shot of busy site traffic passing the same spot repeatedly

scenes.script_line: Have you ever seen something like that? Most of us have. Now imagine a sixth person arrives. They notice the plastic. They check that it is safe to pick up. They collect it and place it in the correct container. The situation changes. Not because the person is stronger or more important. But because they choose to act. This is our lesson today.

shots.text: worker stopping, checking it is safe, and picking up a piece of litter
close-up of a hand placing litter into the correct container
wide shot of the same path now clear of litter
worker continuing their walk calmly after the small action

scenes.script_line: Change can begin with me. Let's repeat. Change can begin with me. Sometimes, when we see a problem, we think about whose fault it is. Who left this here? Who was supposed to clean it? Why has nobody done anything? Those questions can matter when we need to understand a repeated issue. But there is another question that may help us begin.

shots.text: worker on a team noticing loose packaging collecting near a fence
close-up of a hand securing a loose sheet before the wind lifts it
worker telling a supervisor that a waste container is full
wide shot of a team working steadily with one member pausing to tidy

scenes.script_line: "What can I do safely and usefully right now?" Maybe the answer is to collect a wrapper. Maybe it is to secure a loose sheet before the wind lifts it. Maybe it is to tell the supervisor that a container is full. Different problems need different responses. Responsibility is not doing everything. It is making a thoughtful choice about your part.

shots.text: worker noticing an unknown leaking container and stepping back carefully
shots.pexels: worker noticing leaking container stepping back

shots.text: close-up of a hand holding a radio, calling a supervisor about a hazard
worker keeping others away from a hazard area with a raised hand
trained supervisor arriving to handle a reported hazard safely

scenes.script_line: And there is a very important limit. If you find a chemical spill, a sharp object, damaged electrical equipment or another serious hazard, do not put yourself at risk. Stop nearby unsafe work if appropriate, keep others away and report it immediately. You do not need to become a hero. You need to act responsibly.

shots.text: experienced worker speaking kindly to a new colleague about a left-behind wrapper
close-up of a hand showing a new worker where packaging belongs
new worker nodding and learning, no embarrassment, respectful tone
wide shot of a senior and new worker walking together across the site
shots.pexels: senior new worker walking together site

scenes.script_line: Sometimes the best action is to ask for trained help. Now imagine a colleague who is new to Edenrise. They finish a job and leave a wrapper behind. You could embarrass them in front of the team. You could tell yourself they do not care. Or you could simply say, "We collect all our packaging here. Let me show you." Which response is more likely to help someone learn?

shots.text: worker speaking up at a short team gathering, suggesting a bin be moved
close-up of a hand pointing toward a better spot for a waste bin
supervisor listening attentively and moving the bin closer to the work area
wide shot of the team working more easily after the small change

scenes.script_line: Which one builds trust? We can keep high standards and still speak with respect. That is how a strong team works. Sometimes one person's action is to speak up. "This bin is too far from where we are working. Could we move it?" "We are losing useful pieces of timber. Could we make a reuse area?" "Rain is washing soil onto the path. Could someone check it?"

shots.text: quiet, respected worker noticing a small problem early on site
close-up of hands keeping a promise, finishing a task as agreed
worker leaving their work area tidy and ready for the next person
wide shot of colleagues showing quiet respect for a reliable teammate

scenes.script_line: One good question may improve the system for everyone. And managers have a responsibility to listen, provide tools and fix obstacles. It would be unfair to ask workers to meet a standard without giving them the means to do it. Think about the people you respect at work. Perhaps they are not always the loudest. Perhaps they are the ones who notice problems early.

shots.text: worker pausing to notice a small leaking tap during a walk around site
close-up of a dripping tap being checked by hand
worker choosing a safe, useful action in response to a small problem
wide shot of a worker asking for help from a passing colleague

scenes.script_line: Who ask questions when they are unsure. Who keep promises. Who leave their work ready for the next person. They influence the team through what they do. And that influence can begin with ordinary actions. Remember three questions. What do I notice? What can I do safely? Who needs to know? Again. What do I notice? What can I do safely? Who needs to know?

shots.text: worker beginning a small action, collecting a wrapper near a waste container
close-up of a hand emptying a nearly full waste container responsibly
worker treating a colleague with visible respect while working together
wide shot of a team quietly supporting one another on a calm worksite
shots.pexels: team supporting each other calm worksite

scenes.script_line: These questions give us a simple way to respond without blame or panic. Tomorrow, perhaps you will see something small that needs attention. A wrapper. A leaking tap. A waste container that needs emptying. You may not be able to solve the whole problem yourself. But you can begin. Choose a useful action. Ask for help when needed. And treat other people with respect. Because change can begin with me.

shots.text: worker crouching beside a small problem, deciding how to respond calmly
close-up of a hand reaching for a radio to tell a supervisor
wide shot of a worker weighing what they can safely do alone on site
two workers quietly agreeing on the next respectful step together

scenes.script_line: And it becomes even stronger when we choose to act together. In our final lesson, we will look beyond today's work and ask what kind of place we want to leave for the future.
